newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom issue price seen as fair.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom issue price seen as fair.

text.p: German phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG, setting the issue price for its global share offering at 28.50 marks, has met the low end of expectations and left room for future price gains, analysts said on Sunday.
Nicole Cousins, telecom analyst at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, said she believed the lower-than-expected price for the issue meant there was a good chance of price gains once trading began.
"We thought it would come in at the high end of the range (30 marks)," she said. "Based on our benchmarks, we thought it was fairly valued at 30 marks," she said.

Jonathan Shantry, European telecom analyst for Credit Lyonnais in London, said the pricing guaranteed a good value for small investors because the return would be close to the six percent offered by German bonds.
"There is room for more gains. The share price could go up to around 33 marks, at which point institutions will probably begin taking profits," he said. "The fair value is 30 marks."
Shantry said the absolute ceiling for Telekom's share price should be around 35 marks. He also thought individual investors were unlikely to sell their Telekom shares quickly.
Telekom shares will begin trading for the first time on November 18 in Germany and New York, where they will be issued at $18.89, and a day later in Tokyo.

Telekom, Europe's largest telephone company with annual sales of 66 billion marks, placed a total of 713 million shares. This included a basic allotment of 600 million shares, another 90 million shares in the so-called Greenshoe, or overallotment, and up to 30 million shares for employees.
The seven million share discrepancy between the total shares on offer and those placed was due to undersubscription in the employee portion.

Two-thirds of the total issue was placed in Germany and 33 percent abroad, with the largest chunk going to North and South America. More than half the issue was taken by institutional investors, while around two million retail investors subscribed to the issue.
Vereins- und Westbank AG said in a statement that the price was fair because the issue was oversubscribed five times.

The bank "considers the great interest on the part of foreign investors not only a statement of trust in Telekom but also in Germany as an industrial centre," adding that institutional investors would quickly buy more Telekom shares.
But German small investor lobby group Schutzgemeinschaft der Kleinaktionaere (SdK) said the price was too expensive.

In a statement, the lobby group said it had already warned that the 25-30 mark range set for book-building bids for the stock was pitched too high. "The SdK would have considered an issue price of about 20 marks per share appropriate," it said.
The group said it was evident that larger investors had pushed the price higher.
"A small investor had little influence on the price as his standard bid is 'cheapest'," it said.

The SdK said it believed the price Telekom employees will pay for stock -- at a 40 percent discount to the 28.50 mark issue price -- was more appropriate, but noted that this part of the issue had been undersubscribed.

Bruno Hidding, equities analyst with Hoppenstedt Verlag, said the subscription price in the premarketing phase was indicated at just 25 marks. At 28.50 marks, Telekom was valued at 14 times its earnings, higher than most international telecommunications companies.
"The T-share with an issue price of 28.50 is not cheap -- it's expensive. Should the initial demand push the share price up to 35 marks and higher, take your profits," he said.
